plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: The split between open creative questions and exact, checkable facts. Genre, perspective and the whole design were mine to decide, while the 'This computer' section and the hub's protocol page with its automatic harness told me exactly what would run and how it would be judged. That let me test the plan's riskiest claims on the real machine instead of guessing. 'What this computer doesn't have', with a stand-in for each missing thing, was especially useful.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Four things. First, 'Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': the hub's protocol page only covers sessions and says the game is not affected outside one, so it doesn't define multiplayer on its own. I read it as couch play on one screen, from a line in the hub repo's docs/multiplayer-plan.md, but that is my inference. Second, 'the engine's native style' and 'the engine's asset library' don't map onto Three.js, which has neither. Third, TASK.md is written to the builder (file names, model line, exit interview, About screen) while STAGE.md asks for a plan, so I had to work out which parts apply at this stage. Fourth, the 'This computer' section is misleading on two points. It lists WebGPU as working with three flags, but with those flags Three's device was lost 0.2 s after startup while frames kept counting, which I first took for real 60 fps. And it lists Firefox as WebGL 2, but headless Firefox refused a WebGL2 context here (AllowWebgl2:false); it only worked headed under xvfb-run.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Translating a game whose identity is a physical balance board into something a thumb on a stick can't trivially beat, while keeping it original. My first test showed that simply parking the stick on the target scored 100%, because a thumb is far steadier than a body, and it took a slow-sway model to make holding still a real game. Getting the numbers right was close behind: when I simulated each event with bots, most of my first values were wrong, some badly (nobody could lose Plate Spinners, nobody could win Tug of Peace, one Check-In test was impossible, and Plate Spinners couldn't be played on keys at all). Knowing when something was really proven was hard too: the wiring problems only appeared when I built one event through everything from the plan's own recipes, including tests that had been passing on a dead WebGPU device. Writing for builders whose capability and budget I don't know is why the plan has a build order and a cut order. And I can't hear anything here, so the music and voices are specified by theory and only checked as signals.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Fix the WebGPU line in 'This computer': add --use-vulkan=swiftshader --use-angle=swiftshader to the listed flags, and warn that the listed flags alone lose the device within a second while frames keep counting, and that real frames run at about 6 fps. That one line would save every builder from testing nothing. State what multiplayer on its own means, for example 'up to four controllers on one screen is required'. Reword Art Direction for an engine with no native style or asset library. Say how capable the builders are and what budget they have, so a plan can be scoped to them. Mark which TASK.md sections apply at the plan stage. On the hub page, state the 60 and 80 character limits on goal and how-to, which are only in retrofit.md, and that progress and ghost traffic must start within the first few seconds of play, because a game with a long intro fails the harness.

goalReason: PLAN.md exists and covers most of TASK.md, but the transcript does not show every requirement is covered. The plan itself labels audio being heard and real controller/TV play as unverified stand-ins, and the About/Credits screen, exit-interview file and chat report are written as instructions for a future builder rather than as answers. The coverage claims also changed across turns and rest on judgement-based clause pairing, so there is no stable evidence of full coverage.
